knob-and-tube-wiring.title: Knob-and-tube wiring
knob-and-tube-wiring.hook: The original wiring in many pre-war houses has no ground wire, and plenty of insurers won't cover it.
knob-and-tube-wiring.summary: The earliest standard house wiring ran single cloth-covered wires through ceramic knobs and tubes. Its insulation is now 80 to 140 years old, it has no ground, and it was never meant to be buried in insulation. Many houses were rewired in part, which can leave live sections hidden in walls and attics.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: A house wired between 1900 and 1930 almost certainly started with it. No count exists of how many still have live sections.

check: Look at the basement ceiling and in the attic for white ceramic knobs nailed to joists and ceramic tubes through them.
Look for pairs of separate cloth-covered wires running a few inches apart.
Two-prong outlets, push-button switches and a fuse box are supporting clues.
Modern cable at the panel does not rule it out: it is often spliced in further along.
knob-and-tube-wiring.action: Have a licensed electrician trace which circuits are still live and quote replacing them. Call your insurer before you buy.
knob-and-tube-wiring.caveat: The end date is soft. Most builders had moved on by about 1930; some rural and low-cost houses used it into the 1940s.

aluminum-branch-wiring.title: Aluminum branch wiring
aluminum-branch-wiring.hook: For about eight years, many houses were wired with aluminum instead of copper, and its connections can overheat.
aluminum-branch-wiring.summary: When copper prices spiked in the mid-1960s, builders wired outlets and switches with aluminum. At ordinary devices the connections loosen and oxidize over time and can get hot enough to start a fire. Repairs are well understood and far cheaper than rewiring.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: CPSC estimated about two million homes were wired with it. Most houses of these years used copper.

check: In the basement, attic or garage, read the printing on exposed cable: look for "AL" or "Aluminum".
At the panel, see whether the thin branch wires are silver rather than copper colored.
Warm or discolored outlet covers and flickering lights are warning signs.
aluminum-branch-wiring.action: Ask an electrician about repairing the connections with approved connectors. Do not swap outlets yourself.
aluminum-branch-wiring.caveat: Large aluminum feeder cables to the panel and to big appliances are normal and are a different matter.

fpe-stab-lok-panels.title: Federal Pacific Stab-Lok panels
fpe-stab-lok-panels.hook: A common breaker panel of the period has breakers that, in testing, often failed to trip.
fpe-stab-lok-panels.summary: Federal Pacific Electric sold millions of Stab-Lok panels. Independent testing found many of its breakers did not trip under overload, which is the one job a breaker has. The company is gone, so replacement is the owner's cost.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Sold in very large numbers, but no count exists of how many remain in service.

check: Open the panel door and look for "Federal Pacific", "FPE" or "Stab-Lok" on the label.
Stab-Lok breakers are thin with a red or orange stripe across the handle.
Do not remove the inner cover yourself.
fpe-stab-lok-panels.action: Get a quote from a licensed electrician to replace the panel. Many inspectors and insurers flag it.

lead-based-paint.title: Lead-based paint
lead-based-paint.hook: Most houses built before 1940 have some lead paint, and sanding it is the dangerous part.
lead-based-paint.summary: Lead paint was used inside and out until it was banned for homes in 1978. Intact paint is a low risk. Peeling paint, windows and doors that rub, and any sanding or demolition create lead dust, which is a serious hazard for young children.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: EPA: 87% of homes built before 1940 and 24% of homes built 1960 to 1978 have some lead-based paint.

check: Look at original windows, doors, trim and porch paint for chipping or a cracked, scaly pattern.
Ask the seller for the federal lead disclosure form, which is required for pre-1978 houses.
Only a lab test or a certified inspector's XRF reading can confirm it.
lead-based-paint.action: Before any sanding or demolition, test first and hire a lead-safe certified contractor.
lead-based-paint.caveat: Paint made before the ban could still be applied in 1978 and a little later.

asbestos-popcorn-ceiling.title: Asbestos in popcorn ceilings
asbestos-popcorn-ceiling.hook: That bumpy ceiling texture may contain asbestos; leave it alone until it's tested.
asbestos-popcorn-ceiling.summary: Spray-on acoustic ceiling texture often contained asbestos until the late 1970s. Undisturbed, it is a low risk. Scraping, drilling or water damage releases fibers.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists of how many textured ceilings contain asbestos.

check: Look for a white, cottage-cheese-like texture on ceilings.
Note any water stains or crumbling.
Only a lab test of a sample can tell you.
asbestos-popcorn-ceiling.action: Do not scrape it. If you plan to remodel, have a sample tested by an accredited lab first.

polybutylene-supply.title: Polybutylene water pipes
polybutylene-supply.hook: Gray plastic water pipe from these years can fail without warning, and some insurers won't cover it.
polybutylene-supply.summary: Polybutylene was a cheap plastic supply pipe used widely from the late 1970s to the mid-1990s. Its fittings and the pipe itself can crack from the inside, leading to sudden leaks. A national settlement covered some replacements; that program has closed.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Estimates of 6 to 10 million homes are often repeated, but no figure was confirmed at a primary source.

check: At the water heater, under sinks and at the main shutoff, look for flexible gray (sometimes blue or black) pipe.
Look for the letters "PB2110" printed on the pipe.
Check for crimp rings of copper or aluminum at fittings.
polybutylene-supply.action: Get a repipe quote and ask your insurer whether they will cover it.

kitec-plumbing.title: Kitec plumbing
kitec-plumbing.hook: Bright orange and blue water pipe from the late 1990s can corrode at its brass fittings.
kitec-plumbing.summary: Kitec was an aluminum-plastic composite pipe with brass fittings. The fittings can lose zinc and clog or break, causing leaks. A class settlement covered replacements; its claim period has ended.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: Used in a minority of houses, more often in the Southwest and in multi-family buildings.

check: At the water heater and main shutoff, look for orange (hot) and blue (cold) pipe.
Look for "Kitec", "PlumbBetter" or "XPA" printed on the pipe.
Look for green or white crust on brass fittings.
kitec-plumbing.action: Have a plumber assess the fittings and quote a repipe.

gfci-protection-milestones.title: No shock protection at wet outlets (GFCI)
gfci-protection-milestones.hook: Outlets near water in older houses usually lack the test-and-reset protection that prevents electrocution.
gfci-protection-milestones.summary: Ground-fault outlets cut power in a fraction of a second when current leaks, preventing most electrocutions near water. The electrical code added them room by room: outdoors and in bathrooms in the 1970s, kitchens in 1987, and more since. A house keeps whatever it was built with unless someone added them.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Original wiring of this age had none at kitchen counters. Many owners have added them since.

check: Look for outlets with TEST and RESET buttons in the kitchen, bathrooms, garage and outside.
Press TEST: the outlet, and any outlets downstream of it, should go dead.
Check the panel for breakers with a test button.
gfci-protection-milestones.action: Adding GFCI outlets or breakers is cheap. Have an electrician do it if you are unsure.
gfci-protection-milestones.caveat: Dates are electrical code editions. States adopted each edition at different times, often years later.

afci-protection-milestones.title: No arc-fault breakers
afci-protection-milestones.hook: Houses built before the early 2000s have no breakers that catch the sparking that starts wiring fires.
afci-protection-milestones.summary: Arc-fault breakers sense the electrical signature of damaged wires or cords and shut the circuit off before a fire starts. They were required for bedrooms from 2002 and for most living areas from 2008.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Almost no houses were built with them before the code required it.

check: At the panel, look for breakers with a TEST button labeled AFCI or Arc Fault.
Ordinary breakers have no test button.
afci-protection-milestones.action: Ask an electrician whether adding arc-fault breakers to bedroom circuits is practical in your panel.
afci-protection-milestones.caveat: Some states delayed or amended the requirement.

problem-chinese-drywall.title: Problem drywall from China
problem-chinese-drywall.hook: Drywall imported during the mid-2000s housing boom gave off sulfur gases that corroded wiring and AC coils.
problem-chinese-drywall.summary: Some drywall imported between about 2001 and 2009 emitted sulfur gases. Homes reported a rotten-egg smell, blackened copper wiring and repeated air-conditioner coil failures. Federal agencies issued a remediation protocol.

prevalence.label: rare
prevalence.note: CPSC received about 4,000 reports, concentrated in Florida, Louisiana and Virginia.

check: Notice any persistent sulfur or rotten-egg smell.
Look at bare copper ground wires behind an outlet cover: black and sooty instead of shiny.
Ask about repeated air-conditioner coil replacements.
problem-chinese-drywall.action: If you see the signs, have it assessed using the CPSC and HUD identification guidance before buying.

unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.title: House not bolted to its foundation
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.hook: In earthquake country, older houses on raised foundations were often never bolted down.
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.summary: Many older wood houses on crawl spaces sit on the foundation without anchor bolts, and the short walls under the floor have no bracing. In a strong earthquake the house can slide off. The retrofit is well understood and relatively cheap.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Only houses on raised foundations are affected, and many have been retrofitted. No statewide count exists.

check: In the crawl space, look along the top of the concrete for bolts with nuts every 4 to 6 feet.
If there is a short stud wall under the floor, see whether plywood is nailed to it.
Houses on a concrete slab do not have this problem.
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.action: Ask a contractor about a brace-and-bolt retrofit. California runs a grant program for eligible ZIP codes.

r22-air-conditioner.title: Air conditioner using R-22
r22-air-conditioner.hook: An original AC from before 2010 runs on a refrigerant that is no longer made.
r22-air-conditioner.summary: Central air conditioners and heat pumps made before 2010 use R-22. US production ended in 2020, so a leak means expensive recovered refrigerant. Units this old are also at or past their normal life.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Nearly all central AC made before 2010 used it, but most original units have since been replaced.

check: Read the data plate on the outdoor unit for "R-22" or "HCFC-22".
The manufacture date is usually on the same plate.
r22-air-conditioner.action: Budget for replacement rather than repeated recharges.

square-d-qo-pon-recall-2020-2022.title: Recalled Square D QO plug-on neutral panels
square-d-qo-pon-recall-2020-2022.hook: About 1.4 million panels made from 2020 to early 2022 were recalled, and the fix is free.
square-d-qo-pon-recall-2020-2022.summary: Schneider Electric recalled Square D QO plug-on neutral load centers because a loose connection can overheat. It matters for houses built or re-paneled in 2020 to 2022.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: About 1.4 million units were sold, out of a much larger market.

check: Open the panel door and look for "Square D", "QO" and "Plug-on Neutral" on the label.
Note the catalog number and date code and compare them with the recall list.
square-d-qo-pon-recall-2020-2022.action: Contact Schneider Electric for the free inspection and repair.
square-d-qo-pon-recall-2020-2022.caveat: Installation can trail manufacture by months, so houses finished in 2023 may also be affected.

radon.title: Radon
radon.hook: Any house of any age can have radon; a cheap test is the only way to know.
radon.summary: Radon is a radioactive soil gas that seeps in through foundations and is the leading cause of lung cancer in non-smokers. It is not tied to an era. Fixes are well established.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: EPA estimates about 1 in 15 homes has elevated radon.

check: Test with a short-term kit in the lowest lived-in level.
A PVC pipe from the slab up through the roof with a small gauge means a system is already installed.
radon.action: If the test is high, get quotes from a certified radon mitigator.

carbon-monoxide-alarms.title: No carbon monoxide alarms
carbon-monoxide-alarms.hook: Houses built before CO alarms were required often have none, even with gas appliances.
carbon-monoxide-alarms.summary: Model codes added carbon monoxide alarms for new homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage in 2009. Older houses often have none unless a state law required them later.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: No national count exists; many states now require them at sale.

check: Look outside each sleeping area for a unit labeled carbon monoxide.
Check the date on any alarm: they expire after 5 to 10 years.
carbon-monoxide-alarms.action: Add CO alarms outside bedrooms and on each level. They cost little.
